messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Public Transport: Bus riding, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh is a 27-year-old Vietnamese American journalist who presents with a PCL-5 score of 64 following a period of sustained physical abuse by a former male romantic partner that ended approximately fourteen months ago. He is currently in a new relationship and works for a mid-sized urban news outlet, a role that requires him to move through the city daily, attend press briefings, and conduct in-person interviews — an environment that has become, for him, a landscape of hidden threat.

The abuse unfolded over nearly two years and escalated gradually. His former partner would strike him without warning — across the face, against the ribs, once throwing him against a kitchen counter so hard that he lost his footing. What made it particularly disorienting was the silence that followed: no explanation, no acknowledgment, just the resumption of ordinary life. Minh learned to read the smallest signals — a delay in a reply, a pause before a door opened — as harbingers of what might come. He was rarely wrong, and that vigilance became the architecture of his days.

Now, when something takes longer than expected — a source who doesn't call back on time, a delayed subway car — Minh finds himself certain that something bad is unfolding, his chest tightening in the same way it did when he would hear footsteps approaching the bedroom. He wakes in the night to check that his apartment door is locked, sometimes two or three times, and even after confirming it, he cannot fully accept that he is safe. This inability to trust reassurance is not stubbornness; it is what the abuse taught him, that safety is always provisional. These beliefs — that people cannot be trusted, that he is fundamentally inadequate for having stayed, that harm can come from anyone — keep his nervous system scanning constantly, which means that ordinary encounters are pre-loaded with threat before they begin.

It is the memory itself that most insistently feeds this worldview. When it returns — and it returns without invitation — it does not feel historical. Minh describes it as happening now, in the room, in his body. He feels physical pain in his ribs and jaw, the same locations where he was struck, and the emotional overwhelm is so total that he has had to step away from his desk mid-story, unable to continue. These intrusions do not leave him thinking about the past; they confirm, in the present tense, that he is the kind of person to whom this happens, and that the world is the kind of place where it does. The memory thus continuously refreshes his conviction that he is inadequate and that no one can be trusted — and those convictions in turn make the world feel perpetually unsafe, sustaining a vigilance that makes it harder for the memories to recede.

Riding the bus to assignments, Minh sits near the exit and watches the other passengers. Being alone with men — in an elevator, in a waiting room, in the back of a rideshare — produces an acute alertness that he cannot reason his way out of, even when the situation is mundane. When these moments arrive, or when a trauma-related event surfaces in his reporting — a story about domestic violence, a photograph of a bruised face — the memories flood back with particular force. In response, Minh has developed a set of habits that feel like self-protection. He dwells obsessively on what he did wrong in the relationship, replaying choices as though understanding them might inoculate him against repetition. He suppresses any anger he feels, afraid that expressing it would make him dangerous or make him like his former partner. He has begun restricting what he eats, a behaviour he cannot fully explain but that feels like control over the one thing that remains his. These strategies, however, have quietly deepened his sense of himself as broken and unworthy, reinforcing the very beliefs they were meant to quiet.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago. He was interviewing a male official in a small conference room and found himself unable to speak — his body had decided, without consulting him, that he was back in that kitchen. His editor noticed. Minh is afraid, above all, that he will never feel safe in his own body again. What he hopes for, tentatively, is that the past might one day feel like the past.
